text: Translate: **Every student loves some course.** ($student(x)$: $x$ is a student; $course(y)$: $y$ is a course; $loves(x,y)$: $x$ loves $y$.)
solution: “Every student” is a universal over students: ∀x(student(x) → …) — with →, because non-students satisfy it vacuously.
“… loves some course” is an existential inside: ∃y(course(y) ∧ loves(x,y)) — with ∧, because we need a course that is loved.
So the formula is ∀x(student(x) → ∃y(course(y) ∧ loves(x,y))).

common_wrong.why: ∀x(student(x) ∧ …) would claim every object is a student.
Puts the course outside the student scope: one course loved by all students.
∀y says every course, not some course.

text: Which formula says **“No A is B”**?
solution: “No A is B” = there does not exist an x that is both A and B: ¬∃x(A(x) ∧ B(x)).
Equivalently ∀x(A(x) → ¬B(x)): every A is not B.

common_wrong.why: That says some A is B — the opposite.
∀x(A∧¬B) claims every object is A and not B.
∃x(¬A∨B) is true whenever some object is not A or is B.

text: Domain $D = \{a, b, c, d\}$, relation $R = \{(a,b), (b,a), (c,d)\}$. How many ordered pairs $(x, y)$ satisfy $R(x, y) \wedge x \neq y$?
solution: List the pairs of R: (a,b), (b,a), (c,d).
Each has x ≠ y (a≠b, b≠a, c≠d), so all 3 satisfy R(x,y) ∧ x≠y.
concept: Counting pairs in a relation on a finite domain.

common_wrong.why: That counts ordered pairs of the whole D×D with x≠y (4·3 = 12) or similar; only pairs in R count.

text: The free variables of $\forall x\,(P(x) \vee Q(x, y)) \wedge R(y)$ are:
solution: ∀x binds every x in its scope P(x)∨Q(x,y).
The y in Q(x,y) is inside the ∀x scope but not bound by it (different variable); the y in R(y) is outside all scopes. So y is free, x is bound.

common_wrong.why: x is bound by ∀x.
y is free, so it is not a sentence.
x is bound.

text:
Which of I–IV are logically equivalent to $
eg \exists x\,(P(x) \wedge Q(x))$?  I. $ orall x\,
eg(P(x) \wedge Q(x))$   II. $ orall x\,(P(x) ightarrow 
eg Q(x))$   III. $\exists x\,
eg(P(x) \wedge Q(x))$   IV. $ orall x\,(
eg P(x) \vee 
eg Q(x))$
solution: ¬∃xφ ≡ ∀x¬φ (De Morgan for quantifiers): I is equivalent.
¬(P∧Q) ≡ P→¬Q ≡ ¬P∨¬Q, so II and IV are equivalent too. III keeps the ∃, so it is not.

common_wrong.why: III still has ∃ — ¬∃ is not ∃¬.
III is not equivalent.

text: Over the domain $\{1, 2, \dots, 8\}$, let $prime(x)$ mean $x$ is prime and let $P(x)$ be $\forall y\,(y \mid x \rightarrow (y = 1 \vee y = x)) \wedge x > 1$. How many elements $x$ of the domain satisfy $P(x)$?
solution: P(x) says: every divisor y of x is 1 or x, and x > 1 — exactly the definition of prime.
Primes in 1..8: 2, 3, 5, 7 → 4 elements.

common_wrong.why: Forgetting 2 is prime, or counting 1 (but x>1 excludes 1).
Counting 1 as prime; the x>1 clause excludes it.

text: Domain $\{a, b\}$, relation $R = \{(a,b), (b,a)\}$. Which statement is true?

options.t: Both $\forall x\exists y\,R(x,y)$ and $\exists y\forall x\,R(x,y)$ are true
$\forall x\exists y\,R(x,y)$ is true, $\exists y\forall x\,R(x,y)$ is false
$\exists y\forall x\,R(x,y)$ is true, $\forall x\exists y\,R(x,y)$ is false

solution: ∀x∃yR(x,y): for x=a, y=b works; for x=b, y=a works → true.
∃y∀xR(x,y): y=a needs R(a,a) and R(b,a) — R(a,a) is absent → false; y=b needs R(a,b), R(b,b) — R(b,b) absent → false. So false.
concept: Order of quantifiers on a small grid.

common_wrong.why: No single y is related to both a and b.
The ∃∀ direction is the stronger one; it fails here.

text: The negation of $\forall x\,\exists y\,R(x,y)$ is:
solution: ¬∀xφ ≡ ∃x¬φ, then ¬∃yψ ≡ ∀y¬ψ:  ¬∀x∃yR(x,y) ≡ ∃x∀y¬R(x,y).

common_wrong.why: Keeps the ∀ outside: ¬∀x∃y is not ∀x∃y¬.
∃∃ — both quantifiers must flip.
∀∀ — the outer ∀ must become ∃.

text:
Which formulas say **“at most two elements satisfy P”**?  I. $ orall x orall y orall z\,((P(x)\wedge P(y)\wedge P(z)) ightarrow (x=y \vee y=z \vee z=x))$   II. $
eg\exists x\exists y\exists z\,(P(x)\wedge P(y)\wedge P(z)\wedge x
eq y \wedge y
eq z \wedge z
eq x)$   III. $\exists x\exists y\,(P(x)\wedge P(y)\wedge x
eq y)$   IV. $ orall x orall y\,((P(x)\wedge P(y)) ightarrow x=y)$
solution: “At most two P's”: any three P-elements must contain a repeat — that is I. Equivalently, it is NOT the case that three distinct P's exist — II.
III says at least two (wrong); IV says at most one (stronger, wrong).
concept: At most n = any n+1 elements contain a pair equal.

common_wrong.why: IV is “at most one”, not “at most two”.
III is “at least two”.

text: Domain $\{1, \dots, 6\}$, $P(x)$ = “$x$ is even”. How many elements are witnesses of $\exists x\,P(x)$ (i.e. satisfy $P$)?
solution: Even numbers in 1..6: 2, 4, 6 → 3 witnesses.
concept: ∃ over a finite domain = big OR; witnesses.

common_wrong.why: Counting only 2 and 4 and forgetting 6.

text: “**Only** A are B” means:
solution: “Only A are B”: if something is B, it must be A — every B is an A: ∀x(B(x) → A(x)).
“All A are B” would be ∀x(A→B) — the other direction. “All and only” is the biconditional.

common_wrong.why: That is “all A are B”, not “only A are B”.
↔ would also say every A is B.
∃ is far too weak.

text: Edge case: “**Not all** that glitters is gold” ($glitters(x)$, $gold(x)$) is:
solution: “Not all glitters are gold” = it is false that every glittering thing is gold = ¬∀x(glitters→gold) ≡ ∃x(glitters ∧ ¬gold).
A says every glittering thing is NOT gold; B is about gold non-glittering things; D is wrong because C is equivalent.

common_wrong.why: ∀(A→¬B) means NO glittering thing is gold — stronger.
C is exactly equivalent to the negation.

text: Which of the following are **valid** (true in every interpretation, non-empty domains)?  A. $\forall x(P(x) \vee Q(x)) \to (\forall x P(x)) \vee (\forall x Q(x))$   B. $(\exists x (P(x) \wedge Q(x))) \to ((\exists x P(x)) \wedge (\exists x Q(x)))$   C. $\forall x\exists y R(x,y) \to \exists y\forall x R(x,y)$   D. $((\forall x P(x)) \vee (\forall x Q(x))) \to \forall x (P(x) \vee Q(x))$
solution: A is not valid: on U={1,2} with P={1}, Q={2}, LHS is T and RHS is F.
B is valid: a witness for P∧Q is a witness for P and for Q.
C is not valid: the diagonal grid has ∀x∃y true and ∃y∀x false.
D is valid: if all x satisfy P (or all satisfy Q), then all satisfy P∨Q.
concept: One-way quantifier laws; counter-models on 2-element domains.

common_wrong.why: A is the classic trap: ∀ over ∨ does not split.

text: Which assignment on $U = \{1, 2\}$ is a counter-model refuting $\forall x(P(x) \vee Q(x)) \equiv (\forall x P(x)) \vee (\forall x Q(x))$?
solution: Need LHS = ∀x(P∨Q) true and RHS = ∀xP ∨ ∀xQ false.
A: x=1: T∨F=T; x=2: F∨T=T → LHS T. ∀xP fails at 2, ∀xQ fails at 1 → RHS F. Refutes ✓. B: ∀xP=T → RHS T. C: LHS F = RHS F. D: ∀xQ=T → RHS T.

common_wrong.why: ∀xP is true there, so the right side is true — no refutation.

text: How many different interpretations are there for a single unary predicate $P$ over a 2-element domain?
solution: Each of the 2 elements may be in P or not: 2² = 4 interpretations.

common_wrong.why: That counts assignments of a truth value to P as a whole, not its extension.

text: If $x$ is not free in $A$, then $\forall x\,(P(x) \to A)$ is equivalent to:
solution: ∀x(P→A) ≡ (∃xP) → A when x is not free in A: if some x has P, then A must hold; if none does, vacuously true.

common_wrong.why: ∀x(P→A) is NOT (∀xP)→A: with P true somewhere and A false, LHS is false but RHS is true.

text: Which of these is **NOT** valid?

options.t: $\forall x(P(x) \wedge Q(x)) \equiv (\forall x P(x)) \wedge (\forall x Q(x))$
$\exists x(P(x) \vee Q(x)) \equiv (\exists x P(x)) \vee (\exists x Q(x))$
$\forall x(P(x) \to Q(x)) \to ((\forall x P(x)) \to (\forall x Q(x)))$
$\exists x(P(x) \wedge Q(x)) \equiv (\exists x P(x)) \wedge (\exists x Q(x))$

solution: A, B, C are laws (checked on all domains ≤ 3).
D fails: P true only at 1, Q only at 2 on {1,2}: LHS false, RHS true.

common_wrong.why: ∀ DOES distribute over ∧.

text:
Which of I–IV are equivalent to $ orall x\,(P(x) 	o Q(x))$?  I. $ orall x\,(
eg P(x) \vee Q(x))$   II. $
eg\exists x\,(P(x) \wedge 
eg Q(x))$   III. $\exists x\,(
eg P(x) \vee Q(x))$   IV. $ orall x\,(
eg Q(x) 	o 
eg P(x))$
solution: P→Q ≡ ¬P∨Q, so I ✓. ¬∃x(P∧¬Q) ≡ ∀x¬(P∧¬Q) ≡ ∀x(P→Q), so II ✓. III keeps ∃ — ✗. IV is the contrapositive ¬Q→¬P ≡ P→Q — ✓.

common_wrong.why: III has ∃ — an existential is not equivalent to a universal here.

text: A sentence is **satisfiable but not valid** iff:

options.t: true in at least one interpretation and false in at least one

solution: Valid = true in all; satisfiable = true in some; satisfiable-but-not-valid = true in some, false in some.

common_wrong.why: That is 'valid', not 'satisfiable but not valid'.

text: If $\exists s\exists t\exists u\forall v\forall w\forall x\forall y\,\psi$ (ψ quantifier-free) has a model with 7 elements, then necessarily:

options.t: it has no model with ≤ 3 elements
it has no model with > 7 elements
it has at least one model with ≤ 3 elements

solution: ∃*∀* quantifier-free sentences have the small-model property (Bernays–Schönfinkel): if a model of size 7 exists, choose one witness per existential; the remaining ∀ part only needs those ≤ 3 elements.

common_wrong.why: The 7-element model need not be minimal; a smaller one exists.

text: How many different interpretations are there for a single binary predicate $R$ over a 2-element domain?
solution: R is a subset of D×D with 4 pairs; each pair in or out: 2⁴ = 16.
concept: Counting interpretations of a binary predicate.

common_wrong.why: That counts pairs, not subsets of pairs.

text: Over the domain of natural numbers, which ONE is valid?
solution: A is induction over ℕ: base P(0), step upward → all naturals. Valid.
B: the step goes down from 0 — over ℕ the premise is false at x=0 unless P(0) forces…; invalid in general (counter-model P = {0} on ℤ-like readings).
C: base at 1000 with a downward step covers only x ≤ 1000 — not ∀x.
D: base at 1000 with an upward step covers only x ≥ 1000 — not ∀x.
concept: Induction as a first-order axiom; direction matters.

common_wrong.why: From P(1000) upward you only get x ≥ 1000.

text: The logic-program clause  A(x) ← B(x, y), C(y)  as a first-order sentence is:
solution: The head A(x) fires when SOME y satisfies the body: ∀x((∃y(B(x,y)∧C(y))) → A(x)).
A is wrong because ∀y in the body would demand all y's; C asserts A unconditionally; D has the wrong quantifier order.

common_wrong.why: ∀y in the body is too strong: the rule fires for a single witness y.

text: Which are prenex forms of $(\forall x\,P(x)) \vee (\exists y\,Q(y))$?  A. $\forall x\exists y\,(P(x) \vee Q(y))$   B. $\exists y\forall x\,(P(x) \vee Q(y))$   C. $\forall x\forall y\,(P(x) \vee Q(y))$   D. $\exists x\exists y\,(P(x) \vee Q(y))$
solution: Pull the quantifiers out (no shared variables): (∀xP) ∨ (∃yQ) ≡ ∀x∃y(P(x)∨Q(y)) ≡ ∃y∀x(P(x)∨Q(y)) — the two statements A and B are both equivalent prenex forms.

So the correct option is the one reading 'A and B'. C and D are wrong: pulling both quantifiers out as ∀∀ or ∃∃ changes the meaning, since the two parts share no variable and ∨ distributes over the quantifiers in either order.

common_wrong.why: B (the formula ∃y∀x…) is also equivalent — the option 'A only' is wrong because both orders work when the parts share no variable.
